issues.quote: On September 30, it said that finishing the plant will cost significantly more than assumed in June, that it needs additional capital, and that its timeline for green steel is unchanged.
issues.problem: This puts words directly in Stegra's mouth, but the original release was never read (STG2 is Tech.eu plus Finwire only). The 'timeline unchanged' part comes from Finwire alone. The date has no year, and 'will cost' is a forward-looking 'will' in a sentence about a company.
issues.fix: On September 30, 2026, according to reports by Tech.eu and Finwire, Stegra said the cost of completing the plant is significantly higher than it assumed in June and that it needs more capital; Finwire reported that its timeline for green steel remains unchanged.

issues.quote: The OECD's own history of that era: optimistic forecasts drew investment into new mills worldwide, and then the first oil shock hit.
issues.problem: Coming right after 'fell by half by 1982', this reads as the cause of the U.S. drop. The OECD passage describes global overcapacity, and C67 says explicitly that it should not be given as the full cause.
issues.fix: The OECD's history describes the worldwide backdrop of that era: optimistic forecasts drew investment into new mills around the world, and then the first oil shock hit. The record doesn't pin America's drop on a single cause.

issues.quote: The reference point named in 2018 was about eighty percent.
issues.problem: This sits between the administration's own claim and two skeptical studies, so it works as the channel scoring the policy (77 vs 80). C33 says not to judge whether the target was met. The 80% figure was already given earlier in the same segment.

issues.quote: a peak in share, not a normal.
issues.problem: 'Peak' is a factual claim about the share across all years. The claims table only has 1944, 1950, 1955 and 1960, so nothing shows that mid-century was the highest U.S. share.
issues.fix: an unusual moment, not a baseline.

issues.quote: and the bill is reduced for free allowances European mills still receive, so no importer pays exactly this.
issues.problem: The caveat leaves out the deduction for carbon price already paid in the producing country (C49, CBAMD), which is another way the real bill differs from this figure.
issues.fix: and the bill is reduced for free allowances European mills still receive, and for any carbon price already paid where the steel was made, so no importer pays exactly this.

issues.quote: The latest change, as of October 2026, came in June.
issues.problem: June 2025 was mentioned just before this, so it is unclear which June is meant.
issues.fix: The latest change, as of October 2026, came in June 2026.

issues.quote: one formal way to ask what happens to steel in an emergency
issues.problem: Section 232 is about national security findings, not emergencies. This describes the law beyond what P9705/C71 say.
issues.fix: one legal route for treating steel imports as a national-security question

issues.quote: studies of earlier U.S. steel tariffs reached different conclusions
issues.problem: The 2018 tariffs are part of the current tariff, so calling them 'earlier' is inaccurate.
issues.fix: studies of the 2002 and 2018 U.S. steel tariffs reached different conclusions

issues.quote: In England, he had seen the Bessemer process for making steel demonstrated, and he decided to build.
issues.problem: Joining the two with 'and' implies that seeing the demonstration caused the decision. C06 doesn't say that.
issues.fix: In England, he had seen the Bessemer process for making steel demonstrated. Later, he decided to build.

issues.quote: That isn't a secret formula. It's geography plus logistics.
issues.problem: Denying a 'secret' still brings up a secrecy frame, and the sentence is unmarked opinion.
issues.fix: Our read: it's geography plus logistics — whoever controls the cheapest path from rock to rail gains an edge that everyone else has to answer.

issues.quote: That's "steel as national power" in numbers: a share.
issues.problem: This is the channel's interpretation, but it sits before the 'Our read' marker.
issues.fix: Our read: that's "steel as national power" in numbers — a share. Part of it came from a world still rebuilding after the war — an unusual moment, not a baseline.

issues.quote: — the same idea of steel as power, now in many more countries.
issues.problem: The channel's own gloss is added onto an OECD finding with no opinion marker, so it reads as part of what the OECD said.
issues.fix: End the OECD sentence at 'industry.' and add: 'Our read: that's the same idea of steel as power, now held in many more countries.'

issues.problem: This overstates things: BF-BOF and EAF output differ in product mix. The WSIF figures are per tonne of crude steel.
issues.fix: Same unit — a tonne of crude steel — different route
Add a CARN line to C15 that names Frick as running the company, or cut 'run by Henry Frick'.

issues.problem: C43 doesn't say there was a new review before the June 13, 2025 order.
issues.fix: Add a CRS citation to C43, or cut 'After a new review,'.

issues.quote: stop processing steel slabs at its Granite City plant in Illinois
issues.problem: C47 doesn't cover 'slabs' or 'Illinois'. The AP headline says 'processing steel'.
issues.fix: Confirm 'slabs' and 'Illinois' in the AP text and add them to C47, or use: 'stop processing steel at its Granite City plant'.

issues.quote: In 2025, about eighty-two million: four percent.
issues.problem: C03 gives 4.43%. Every other use says 'about four percent', but here it is stated as exact.
issues.fix: In 2025, about eighty-two million: about four percent.

issues.problem: Ownership is ongoing, and there is no SEC filing after 2025 (see the C57 risk note). The status needs a date.

Seg 09: Granite City details 'steel slabs' and 'in Illinois'.

strengths: The disclaimer uses the exact G §4 wording and comes at about 0:15, inside the first 30 s.
All three myth vs record beats are stated neutrally with no named speakers, and each ends with a measured conclusion ('something narrower', 'sits in between').
The golden share segment says the NSA 'has not been made public' instead of guessing at its contents, and uses 'consent rights' rather than 'veto'.
The cross-basis comparisons are handled: USGS raw vs worldsteel crude (checked to match for 2021), exports vs crude output marked 'by weight', and CO₂ from 2024 data at the 2026 price stated openly.
The CBAM illustration is labelled as the channel's own calculation, gives its formula inputs, says no importer pays exactly this, and names the free-allowance adjustment and default values.
The OECD 745 Mt figure is presented as a projection by a named organization. No predictions in the channel's own voice; Stegra gets 'We won't guess whether or when it opens.'
Biden's and Trump's orders get the same neutral wording, and policy results are attributed ('in the Commerce Secretary's opinion', 'CRS notes').
Carnegie material is consistently marked as his own account ('Carnegie wrote/recalled'), and the Homestead passage stays close to the wording of the PHMC marker.
China figures are attributed to the OECD and presented as institutional data, not national generalizations.
The closing line 'Whether that is worth what it costs, these numbers can't settle' avoids taking a policy side.
